questions.stem: A random variable is best described as…
options: a number that changes whenever you look
the probability attached to every single outcome
a function from outcomes to real numbers
a set of outcomes sharing one property
questions.correctFeedback: Right — X(ω) takes an outcome and returns a number. Probability isn't part of the definition.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It's a function: outcome in, real number out. The probabilities belong to the sample space; the variable just carries them.

questions.stem: Three fair coin tosses, X = number of heads. P(X < 2) equals…
options: four over eight, the height before the jump
seven over eight, the height after the jump
three over eight, the jump size at two
one over eight, the height at zero heads
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — X < 2 means 0 or 1 heads: 1/8 + 3/8 = 4/8. That's F(2−), the level just before the jump at 2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: X < 2 means 0 or 1 heads, so 1/8 + 3/8 = 4/8 — the level just before the jump. F(2) = 7/8 would be P(X ≤ 2).

questions.stem: Which of these could NOT be a distribution function?
options: one that is flat, then jumps, then stays flat
one that rises smoothly from zero up to one
one that jumps at every integer up to 1
one that rises to 0.9, then dips to 0.8
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — a running total of probability can never go down. Any dip breaks the non-decreasing property.
questions.incorrectFeedback: A d.f. may jump or rise smoothly, but it can never decrease. The one that dips from 0.9 to 0.8 is invalid.

questions.stem: From Lesson 2: events A and B each have positive probability and cannot occur together. Then A and B are…
options: independent, since they share no outcomes
dependent, since one excludes the other
independent, if both their probabilities match
dependent, only if they are exhaustive
questions.correctFeedback: Right — P(A∩B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) > 0, so the product rule fails. Knowing A happened tells you B didn't.
questions.incorrectFeedback: They're dependent: P(A∩B) = 0 while P(A)P(B) > 0. Mutually exclusive is the opposite of independent here, not the same thing.
